sources.entry: Maker's Schedule, Manager's Schedule - Paul Graham *(Y Combinator)*

summary.title: Maker's Schedule, Manager's Schedule
summary.one_liner: Meetings cost makers (programmers, writers) far more than managers because makers work in half-day blocks, and office hours can contain meetings without breaking a maker's day.
takeaways: Managers schedule time in one-hour slots, while makers need units of at least half a day to do deep work.
A single meeting can break a maker's afternoon or morning and can dampen their willingness to start ambitious work.
Office hours clustered at the end of the day let a manager-style schedule coexist with maker-style work time.
Speculative meetings like coffee chats are cheap for managers but costly for makers; the essay suggests making the cost understood.
summary.summary: Paul Graham describes two ways of using time: the manager's schedule, divided into hourly slots and suited to meetings, and the maker's schedule, which needs long uninterrupted blocks. He argues that a meeting costs a maker far more than it costs a manager, since it can wreck half a day and reduce morale for ambitious work. The essay explains how Y Combinator handles this by clustering founder office hours at the end of the day, and mentions his own past habit of programming at night and handling business in the day. It is a short personal essay, not a tutorial, and it offers reasoning and anecdote rather than a formal method.
